# Fixed-camera viewpoints for a tabletop PiPER

**Bottom line.** An overhead camera plus two oblique cameras is a defensible design for *workspace monitoring and independent fingertip triangulation*. It is **not** an arrangement that the policy-learning literature has established as uniquely optimal. Published systems commonly combine a global external view with a front or low-angle view; many also use wrist views. Their papers generally do **not** report reproducible camera heights, distances, or pitch angles. Place the third camera to supply *different visibility and triangulation geometry*, rather than simply another similar-looking image. (zhao2023learningfinegrainedbimanual pages 2-3, chuang2025activevisionmight pages 3-4, khazatsky2024droidalargescale pages 3-4, chuang2025activevisionmight pages 5-6)

## What the cited platforms actually use

| Platform | Reported external viewpoints; distinction from wrist cameras | Published mounting dimensions? |
|---|---|---|
| **Original ALOHA** | One **top** and one **front** fixed Logitech C922x webcam; two additional webcams on the follower wrists. The paper describes four 640 × 480 RGB inputs, not three fixed scene cameras. | No numeric camera height, standoff, or tilt in the cited paper. Its figure’s **60 cm and 50 cm markings depict workspace dimensions**, not camera-mount specifications. (zhao2023learningfinegrainedbimanual pages 3-4, zhao2023learningfinegrainedbimanual pages 2-3) |
| **ALOHA 2** | In the documented ALOHA-2-based AV-ALOHA setup, two fixed Intel RealSense D405 cameras are mounted at the **top and bottom** of the frame, yielding high- and low-angle views; two other D405s are wrist-mounted. AV-ALOHA adds a separately movable stereo camera, which is *not* a fixed viewpoint. | No numeric mount geometry in that account. (chuang2025activevisionmight pages 3-4) |
| **Mobile ALOHA** | One robot-**top-mounted** scene camera and two wrist cameras. The top camera moves *with the mobile base*, so it is not a stationary room camera. | No camera mounting coordinates reported. The figure’s **65–200 cm** numbers are arm reach heights, **100 cm** is arm extension, and **140 cm** is system height—not camera height. (fu2401mobilealohalearning pages 2-4) |
| **DROID** | Two adjustable, exterior, table-mounted **ZED 2 stereo camera units**, plus one wrist-mounted ZED Mini stereo unit. Collectors select external views for each scene, calibrate them, and sometimes move and recalibrate them during data collection. Two stereo units yield four exterior image streams; they are not four independent camera *locations*. | No universal height, distance, or tilt: placement deliberately varies. Extrinsic matrices are recorded for the exterior cameras. (khazatsky2024droidalargescale pages 3-4, khazatsky2024droidalargescale pages 13-15) |
| **RH20T** | **8–10 global cameras** and **1–2 in-hand cameras** per collection platform, with calibrated, synchronized multiview RGB-D observations. This is unusually sensor-rich, not a recommendation to fit ten cameras to a small table. | Camera poses are calibrated per setup; no single standard height/angle is specified in the passages examined. (fang2024rh20tacomprehensive pages 4-5) |
| **Open X-Embodiment** | An **aggregation of different institutions and robot embodiments**, not a physical rig with a standard front, overhead, or shoulder placement. | No collection-wide camera height or tilt can be assigned. (collaboration2310openxembodimentrobotic pages 2-3) |
| **LeRobot SO-100/SO-101** | Robot platforms supported by a **camera-configurable software and dataset ecosystem**, not a standardized camera-mounted benchmark. Community datasets can therefore have different views and camera counts. | No universal SO-10X camera pose follows from the LeRobot paper. (cadene2026lerobotanopensource pages 5-7) |
| **AgileX Cobot Magic** | Published experiments identify an **ALOHA-style bimanual platform**; its use does not itself specify the scene cameras for every experiment. | No defensible platform-wide mounting coordinates in the evidence examined. (wu2024robomindbenchmarkon pages 3-4) |
| **BridgeData V2; robomimic; FurnitureBench** | These names do **not** establish a transferable physical camera pose: robomimic is a simulated demonstration benchmark, whereas the other two involve particular real collection/evaluation setups. The indexed primary papers for these three were not available in this search; I cannot verify a precise fixed-view count or mounting layout for them from the retrieved primary text. | **Do not treat an uncited height or angle attributed to any of these as a published specification.** |

The especially relevant precedent for your layout is **ALOHA 2’s fixed high-plus-low views**, whereas DROID favors **two independently placeable exterior units** and careful per-scene calibration. Neither is a controlled test of your proposed overhead-plus-two-sides configuration. (chuang2025activevisionmight pages 3-4, khazatsky2024droidalargescale pages 3-4)

## Quantitative evidence: view *information* matters more than a universal view ranking

**Camera count and occlusion.** AV-ALOHA trained ACT policies with seven combinations of fixed scene (“Static”), wrist, and *actively repositioned* (“AV”) observations. For the relatively visible simulated **slot-insertion** task, full-task success was **66% Static**, **78% Static + Wrist**, but **36% AV + Static + Wrist**. For **hooking a package**, it was **44% Static**, **30% Static + Wrist**, and **24% with all three sources**. Conversely, for visually challenging **threading**, it was **30% Static**, **52% AV**, and **52% AV + Wrist**; for the real **hidden-pick** task, **40% Static** versus **60% AV + Wrist**, but **15% with all three**. Thus, *more camera inputs are not automatically better*, and views that reveal an otherwise hidden target can be disproportionately useful. These comparisons involve moving cameras and an active-camera control problem—not an ablation of two versus three **fixed** exterior cameras. Simulation results selected the best among 12 checkpoints and used 50 rollouts per checkpoint; real-task configurations used 20 rollouts. (chuang2025activevisionmight pages 5-6, chuang2025activevisionmight pages 4-5, chuang2025activevisionmight pages 3-4)

In a separate multi-view world-model study, adding a **left-shoulder view** to **front + wrist** did **not substantially improve** performance on three evaluated tasks. That is useful evidence of diminishing returns, but it does not test whether adding a *fixed low side view to a top-down-only PiPER rig* helps. (seo2023multiviewmaskedworld pages 19-20)

**Front versus oblique/side.** A 2026 StereoPolicy simulation study evaluated **ten external camera angles** on ToolHang. Relative to a monocular policy, stereo fusion’s reported gains were **18 percentage points at frontview** and **14 points at elevated frontview**; side views benefited less, with the authors attributing this to poorer overlap and self-occlusion. This compares *stereo and monocular methods at each view*, **not** absolute success for overhead versus front versus side; it does not establish that a front camera is always best. On ToolHang with 200 demonstrations, removing wrist observations reduced the stereo policy from **96% to 94%**, while an RGB comparison fell **90% to 86%**. Those figures likewise do not imply that two widely separated Pi camera units will behave like a closely spaced, explicitly fused stereo pair. (han2026stereopolicyimprovingrobotic pages 7-9, han2026stereopolicyimprovingrobotic pages 22-24)

**Shifts after training.** Camera placement is a genuine deployment variable. In a real *cup-on-saucer* test, a policy trained on one third-person pose plus a wrist camera achieved **4/40 full-task successes** aggregated over four changed exterior viewpoints. Novel-view augmentation improved aggregate success to **14/50**, or **20/50** when its view generator was additionally adapted on DROID data. These denominators and viewpoint sets are **not identical**—the unaugmented policy’s fifth-camera result was omitted—so interpret the comparison as evidence of brittleness and useful augmentation, not a clean percentage-point estimate for a specified camera displacement. (tian2024viewinvariantpolicylearning pages 7-8)

In the Colosseum simulated perturbation protocol, front and shoulder cameras’ positions can each change by up to **0.1 m per coordinate** and Euler angles by up to **0.05 rad per coordinate** (about **2.9°**); its real extension also changes and recalibrates the front-camera position. These are *test perturbation ranges*, **not recommended mounting tolerances**. In a separate fixed-camera training study, a conventional simulated behavior-cloning policy scored **0%** on easy and hard camera shifts in three evaluated tasks despite canonical successes of **51.7–63.3%**; a different object-centric 3D method retained task-dependent nonzero success. Because the methods and representations differ, this tests robustness, not an overhead-versus-side ranking. (pumacay2024thecolosseuma pages 4-5, pumacay2024thecolosseuma pages 5-7, zhu2310learninggeneralizablemanipulation pages 6-7)

Evidence specifically for **over-the-shoulder** views is also conditional. A 2026 study deliberately sampled two over-the-shoulder cameras and a wrist view, randomizing calibrated RGB-D camera poses during training. On its Cabinet simulation, its geometry-grounded policy attained **64.4 normalized opening** with randomized cameras versus **39.5** for a camera-conditioned comparison; **normalized opening is not a task-success percentage**. It requires calibrated extrinsics and depth and therefore does not directly predict performance from three uncalibrated RGB-only cameras. **Third, low room-side edge camera.** Keep it sufficiently **oblique and separated in azimuth** from the end-facing view that a fingertip obscured by the gripper, arm, or an object in one side image remains visible in another. A low view contributes evidence of clearance, contact height, and the near side of objects that top-down imagery may conceal; an *extremely* low grazing angle instead risks table-edge occlusion and overlapping fingertips. Position and angle should be chosen by measuring visibility of **both fingertips** across sampled joint configurations, rather than by copying a platform label such as “sideview.” High/low viewpoint complementarity is supported by ALOHA 2’s hardware choice; the need to inspect occlusion is supported by the controlled view experiments. (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000021, pqac-00000024)

**For the few-millimetre drift objective, camera count alone is insufficient.** A back-of-envelope ideal overhead image scale is roughly **2.96 m/4608 ≈ 0.64 mm per pixel** along the wide axis and **1.59 m/2592 ≈ 0.61 mm per pixel** along the narrow axis *at table height*. Those are projected sampling pitches, **not 3D accuracy**: fingertip localization, lens distortion, limited stereo intersection angles, exposure/motion blur, synchronization, and robot-to-camera calibration introduce further error. Calibrate intrinsics and distortion for the actual focus setting, estimate each fixed camera’s extrinsics in one **table/robot-base frame**, and verify *held-out 3D fingertip errors* throughout the reachable volume against a separately measured target. DROID’s repeated extrinsic calibration and RH20T’s multiview camera-to-robot calibration illustrate the distinction between recording extra images and obtaining comparable 3D measurements. Do not fit camera extrinsics to the same potentially drifting joint-angle kinematics you intend to audit without an independent check: doing so can absorb the drift into the calibration. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000015)

**Recommendation.** Install the overhead camera for global clearance and two *nonredundant* oblique cameras for fingertip visibility and depth geometry; the proposed end-facing plus room-side arrangement is a reasonable **starting configuration**, not a literature-validated optimum. First map each camera’s actual field of view and fingertip occlusion over the robot’s working poses; next calibrate and quantify 3D reconstruction error before claiming detection of a few millimetres of kinematic drift. For learned policies, retain consistent camera poses between demonstrations and deployment, and compare overhead-only, overhead + best side, and all three **on your own tasks**. Existing ablations demonstrate that task-dependent visibility helps, added views sometimes add nothing or hurt, and untrained camera shifts can be severe; they do not support a universal prescription of exactly three fixed views. (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000029)

contexts.context: DROID collects 76,000 trajectories across 86 tasks and 564 scenes using a Franka Panda. Its platform has “two adjustable Zed 2 stereo cameras” as exterior/third-person views plus a wrist-mounted Zed Mini. Data collectors freely choose third-person views “that can capture a wide range of interesting behaviors,” then calibrate them with a checkerboard/OpenCV. contexts.context: The excerpt provides camera-view robustness results for han2026stereopolicyimprovingrobotic, specifically for STEREOPOLICY-DP on the TOOLHANG task. The policy is evaluated across 10 camera-angle views, including sideview-left, agentview-left, frontview, agentview-right, sideview-right, and elevated counterparts. Compared with an RGB policy, STEREOPOLICY-DP consistently performs better across all tested views. The largest reported improvements occur in front-facing views: +18% for frontview and +14% for frontview-high. Oblique agentview-left/right views and elevated versions also benefit because stereo helps resolve partial occlusion and spatial correspondence. Side views show smaller gains because of limited overlap and stronger self-occlusion. The excerpt does not report exact success-rate values for each individual camera angle, nor does it provide overhead-versus-side/front/shoulder/wrist numerical comparisons. It also does not present an ablation varying the number of cameras; the relevant method uses left and right stereo images, while the component ablation compares binocular input against feeding the left image to both branches, with success falling from 84.0% to 62.7%. Baseline-distance experiments vary stereo baseline and camera-object distance, rather than camera pose shift magnitude or augmentation. No information is provided here for the other named papers.

contexts.context: The excerpt concerns Tian et al.'s VISTA method for improving policy robustness to altered camera viewpoints. Policies are trained using single-viewpoint RGB robotic trajectory data, while a 3D-aware image diffusion novel-view-synthesis model (ZeroNVS) generates alternate camera views during training. The stated evaluation compares robustness on out-of-distribution viewpoints in simulated and real-world manipulation tasks, with VISTA reported to outperform baselines. The introduction also describes analyses over different viewpoint distributions and experiments finetuning the NVS model with in-domain robotic-task data, including ZeroNVS finetuned on the DROID dataset for real-world policy performance. However, these pages do not provide numerical policy success rates, task-specific success percentages, or ablations isolating named camera positions such as overhead, side, front, shoulder, or wrist. They likewise do not report numerical comparisons by number of cameras or camera-pose shift magnitude. The only explicit methodological comparison in this excerpt is between ordinary single-view training and augmentation with synthesized novel views, plus the distinction between generic and in-domain-finetuned NVS models. VISTA requires neither depth nor camera calibration and does not alter inference-time behavior.

snippets: Upon evaluating the robustness of policies trained with our method to out-of-distribution camera viewpoints, we find that they outperform baselines in both simulated and real-world manipulation tasks.
We take a simple data augmentation approach to this problem by sampling views from a 3D-aware image diffusion novel view synthesis (NVS) model during policy training time.
In training on these augmented views, the policy becomes robust to images from out-of-distribution camera viewpoints.
We refer to this approach as View Synthesis Augmentation (VISTA).
Lastly, policy inference time is not impacted, as we do not modify inference behavior.
Then, we investigate how finetuning an NVS model with in-domain data of robotic tasks can improve downstream policy robustness for held-out tasks.

contexts.context: The excerpt from Chuang et al. (2025) establishes the motivation and experimental framework for comparing active or dynamic camera viewpoints with fixed-camera setups in bimanual robotic manipulation. It states that fixed cameras can suffer from occlusion, limited field of view, and task-agnostic placement, while eye-in-hand cameras may also lose sight of relevant features when objects or fingers obstruct the view. The proposed AV-ALOHA system adds a separate 7-DoF robot arm carrying a stereo camera; the camera viewpoint is controlled through a VR headset and is intended to search for task-relevant views independently of the manipulation arms. The paper evaluates imitation learning in both simulation and real-world settings on tasks emphasizing viewpoint planning, including examples such as peg-in-hole assembly, threading a needle, and inserting a key into a lock. However, pages 1–2 do not provide numerical policy success rates or exact ablation values comparing overhead, side, front, shoulder, or wrist cameras, camera counts, pose-shift magnitudes, or robust viewpoint augmentation. They only preview that ablation studies will examine different camera configurations.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides one camera-view ablation from han2026stereopolicyimprovingrobotic: removing the wrist camera on the ToolHang task using 200 demonstrations. StereoPolicy’s success rate decreases from 96% with the wrist camera to 94% without it, a 2-percentage-point reduction. contexts.context: This excerpt from Tian et al. describes VISTA, a view-augmentation method for improving policy robustness to camera-pose changes between training and deployment. It states that VISTA uses 3D priors from single-image view-synthesis models to augment imitation-learning data, and that experiments in simulated and real environments showed improved robustness to novel viewpoints, especially with synthesis models fine-tuned on robotic data but used zero-shot for the tasks. The passage does not report numerical policy success rates, task-specific overhead/side/front/shoulder/wrist comparisons, camera-count ablations, or quantitative camera-pose-shift magnitudes. Instead, it gives qualitative limitations relevant to interpreting such comparisons: novel-view generation may be computationally expensive; view augmentation can increase training time; sampled poses must cover the deployment viewpoint distribution; and synthesis quality degrades for poses that differ substantially from the original camera. Thus, this excerpt supports the general claim that robust viewpoint augmentation improves camera-pose generalization, but the requested exact numerical comparisons and ablation results are not present in the supplied pages.

contexts.context: AV-ALOHA experiments compared fixed (“Static”), wrist, and an active viewpoint (AV) camera across seven tasks. AV alone was best for pour-test-tube (66% grasp/14% pour) and thread-needle (98% grasp/52% thread), where occlusion and small details mattered. AV found clearer views of holes and box interiors. AV+Static beat Static+Wrist in 5/7 tasks, but all cameras together never ranked top three; extra views sometimes hurt. Fixed cameras helped Group 1 by providing stable pixel-to-object correspondence. Authors conclude AV may suffice broadly, while warning about distribution shift and camera/control complexity.
contexts.question: Setup: a tabletop 6-DOF robot arm (AgileX PiPER, about 0.63 m reach, fingertips reach about 0.76 m at table height) on a 1.29 x 1.36 m table against a wall. We want fixed RGB cameras (Raspberry Pi Camera Module 3 Wide, 102 x 67 deg field of view, 4608 x 2592 px) that (a) triangulate the gripper fingertips to check the arm's joint-angle kinematics (detect drift of a few mm), (b) show whether the workspace is clear, and (c) may later feed learned visuomotor policies. Current proposal: one camera about 1.2 m above the table looking straight down, one about 0.8 m from the arm base past the table end the arm faces at joint 1 = 0, about 0.42 m up and tilted 19 deg down, and a third low camera on the room-side table edge looking toward the wall. Which fixed third-person camera viewpoints do tabletop robot-manipulation datasets and benchmarks use (for example ALOHA / ALOHA 2, Mobile ALOHA, DROID, BridgeData V2, robomimic, FurnitureBench, RH20T, Open X-Embodiment, LeRobot SO-100/SO-101, AgileX Cobot Magic), including camera heights, distances and angles where reported, and what quantitative evidence exists on how viewpoint choice (overhead/top-down, front, side, over-the-shoulder) and the number of fixed views affect visuomotor policy success and robustness to camera shifts? Does the evidence support or contradict an overhead camera plus two side cameras?

contexts.context: VISTA studies viewpoint robustness using novel views sampled on a same-height sphere within a 90° azimuthal “quarter circle arc,” with randomized radius. In real-robot tests, 150 demonstrations from one camera were evaluated at four novel views. Original-data+wrist policies achieved only 14/40 reaching and 4/40 full-task successes (novel-view behavior became “essentially random” for Camera 5). ZeroNVS augmentation improved results to 39/50 and 14/50; DROID-finetuned ZeroNVS reached 44/50 and 20/50. Wrist-only achieved 16/20 and 5/20. DROID finetuning used 3,000 trajectories and four external views from two stereo cameras.

contexts.context: The excerpt evaluates an ALOHA-like system with six cameras: two fixed, two wrist-mounted, and an additional 7-DOF arm camera (“AV”) providing controllable viewpoints. All seven combinations were tested using 50 demonstrations per task; simulation policies were evaluated with 12 checkpoints × 50 rollouts, real-world policies with 20 rollouts. For straightforward tasks (peg, slot, hook), static/non-AV views matched or exceeded AV, and wrist cameras could reduce success. For occluded or precision tasks (threading, pouring, hidden insertion), AV viewpoints improved performance, especially when static cameras could not see critical geometry. No camera heights, distances, angles, or direct overhead-versus-side comparison are reported.

contexts.context: StereoPolicy experiments tested 10 camera angles (side, front, agent/oblique, and elevated variants) on TOOLHANG. StereoPolicy-DP outperformed monocular RGB policies at every angle: gains were largest for front views (“+18%” frontview, “+14%” frontview-high), while side views showed smaller gains because of limited overlap and self-occlusion. Stereo helped resolve occlusions and ambiguous geometry, but performance depended strongly on stereo baseline: optimal baseline/object-distance ratio was \(r=0.09\)–\(0.13\), approximately 10%; at 0.6–0.8 m distance, 6 cm performed well. Two images helped most when fused: success fell from 84.0% to 62.7% when both branches received the same image.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes THE COLOSSEUM benchmark, whose learning setup uses observations from “a given number of cameras”; its 2D baselines use **4 camera RGB views**, while PerAct/RVT use **4-camera RGB-D views** voxelized into a **1.0 m³** workspace with a **100³** grid. The real-world evaluation re-calibrates the **front camera at two different spots** relative to training, explicitly testing camera-pose changes. It reports no camera heights, distances, tilt angles, viewpoint comparisons, or quantitative results isolating overhead versus side/front views or camera count.
contexts.question: Setup: a tabletop 6-DOF robot arm (AgileX PiPER, about 0.63 m reach, fingertips reach about 0.76 m at table height) on a 1.29 x 1.36 m table against a wall. We want fixed RGB cameras (Raspberry Pi Camera Module 3 Wide, 102 x 67 deg field of view, 4608 x 2592 px) that (a) triangulate the gripper fingertips to check the arm's joint-angle kinematics (detect drift of a few mm), (b) show whether the workspace is clear, and (c) may later feed learned visuomotor policies. Current proposal: one camera about 1.2 m above the table looking straight down, one about 0.8 m from the arm base past the table end the arm faces at joint 1 = 0, about 0.42 m up and tilted 19 deg down, and a third low camera on the room-side table edge looking toward the wall. Which fixed third-person camera viewpoints do tabletop robot-manipulation datasets and benchmarks use (for example ALOHA / ALOHA 2, Mobile ALOHA, DROID, BridgeData V2, robomimic, FurnitureBench, RH20T, Open X-Embodiment, LeRobot SO-100/SO-101, AgileX Cobot Magic), including camera heights, distances and angles where reported, and what quantitative evidence exists on how viewpoint choice (overhead/top-down, front, side, over-the-shoulder) and the number of fixed views affect visuomotor policy success and robustness to camera shifts? Does the evidence support or contradict an overhead camera plus two side cameras?

contexts.context: The excerpt evaluates viewpoint generalization, not physical camera placements. Canonical Views reproject RGB-D into fixed virtual cameras; for Cabinet, these are “left and right of the Franka arm to imitate over-the-shoulder views,” while other tasks use two arbitrary training views. Training renders “two over-the-shoulder views and one wrist camera view.” Under randomized cameras, robot-frame 4D RoPE achieved 64.4 normalized opening on Cabinet, 96.7% Pick-Place-Can success, and 29.3% Square Assembly (63.5 average), versus sinusoidal encoding’s 44.1 average. Global compression averaged only 39.7, showing viewpoint changes require spatial/geometric information.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not report camera heights, distances, angles, or fixed-view configurations. It evaluates SpatialVLA across LIBERO and robot setups. Fine-tuned SpatialVLA averages **78.1 ± 0.7%** success, versus OpenVLA **76.5 ± 0.6%**, Octo **75.1 ± 0.6%**, and Diffusion Policy **72.4 ± 0.7%**. On LIBERO-Spatial it achieves **88.2 ± 0.5%**. The authors state that policies lacking integrated depth “face significant challenges” with spatial-layout changes, often below **50%**, and recommend depth or point clouds to improve robustness.

contexts.context: The excerpt proposes robust imitation learning for mobile manipulators using multiple viewpoints and spatial attention, noting that a single internal view can be occluded and that prior work lacked robust multi-view policies. Separate encoders learn task-related viewpoints/regions rather than imposing one camera view. Across tasks/environments, the method improved success by “up to 29.3 points”; focusing on task-related regions improved domain-shift performance by “up to a 33.3-point improvement,” and multi-view training increased occlusion robustness. Fractal-texture augmentation reduces reliance on changing, non-task-related backgrounds, though its computational cost increases with viewpoint count.

contexts.context: The excerpt presents a multi-view policy that learns task-relevant viewpoints rather than assuming one optimal camera. Each of \(M\) viewpoints has its own image encoder, while attention selects useful views and spatial regions. It claims improved robustness to occlusion, distractors, unknown furniture, and domain shifts. Non-task regions are augmented with fractal textures (PixMix), while task regions are detected with FastSAM/CLIP-Adapter and tracked using XMem. Experiments include pick-bottle-from-shelf and place-banana-on-plate tasks under in-distribution and out-of-distribution conditions; the excerpt provides no camera geometry or quantitative success results.

contexts.context: GROOT evaluates camera-angle generalization in three LIBERO simulation tasks, using Canonical, Background-Change, and Camera-Shift conditions (Easy/Hard), with 20 episodes averaged over three seeds. Camera shifts substantially hurt BC-RNN/VIOLA (mostly 0–5% success) and often MAE, while GROOT remains comparatively robust: 81.7/61.7% (moka pot), 71.7/73.3% (frying pan), and 61.7/38.3% (mug) for Camera-Easy/Hard. The excerpt does not report camera heights, distances, azimuth/elevation, number of views, triangulation accuracy, or direct overhead/front/side-view comparisons.

contexts.context: The excerpt evaluates viewpoint-generalization for articulated-object manipulation, not dataset camera layouts. It uses three cameras, sampling 30 real trials (10 per camera pair), and compares fixed versus randomized cameras. On Cabinet normalized opening, out-of-distribution views yielded Plücker Raymaps 29.8±5.2, Canonical Views 45.6±2.3, and GP 51.4±5.2. With fixed/randomized cameras, DP3 scored 50.9±2.0/43.9±1.4, while GP scored 69.1±0.8/64.4±0.8. Unseen elevated/oblique views reduced all performance, but GP retained its advantage. DP3’s small fixed–randomized gap suggests fused point clouds are viewpoint-robust; GP tolerated calibration error but degraded with depth noise.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes ALOHA’s ACT policy using “4 RGB images” (480×640 each) plus joint positions for two 7-DOF arms (14 DOF). A transformer processes image features from all camera viewpoints jointly with proprioception. ACT uses action chunks of length \(k\), predicting a \(k\times14\) action tensor, and temporal ensembling with weights \(w_i=\exp(-m i)\) to smooth overlapping predictions. It states that both chunking and ensembling are important for “precise and smooth motion,” but provides no camera heights, distances, angles, viewpoint ablations, or quantitative evidence comparing overhead, front, side, or over-the-shoulder views.
contexts.question: Setup: a tabletop 6-DOF robot arm (AgileX PiPER, about 0.63 m reach, fingertips reach about 0.76 m at table height) on a 1.29 x 1.36 m table against a wall. We want fixed RGB cameras (Raspberry Pi Camera Module 3 Wide, 102 x 67 deg field of view, 4608 x 2592 px) that (a) triangulate the gripper fingertips to check the arm's joint-angle kinematics (detect drift of a few mm), (b) show whether the workspace is clear, and (c) may later feed learned visuomotor policies. Current proposal: one camera about 1.2 m above the table looking straight down, one about 0.8 m from the arm base past the table end the arm faces at joint 1 = 0, about 0.42 m up and tilted 19 deg down, and a third low camera on the room-side table edge looking toward the wall. Which fixed third-person camera viewpoints do tabletop robot-manipulation datasets and benchmarks use (for example ALOHA / ALOHA 2, Mobile ALOHA, DROID, BridgeData V2, robomimic, FurnitureBench, RH20T, Open X-Embodiment, LeRobot SO-100/SO-101, AgileX Cobot Magic), including camera heights, distances and angles where reported, and what quantitative evidence exists on how viewpoint choice (overhead/top-down, front, side, over-the-shoulder) and the number of fixed views affect visuomotor policy success and robustness to camera shifts? Does the evidence support or contradict an overhead camera plus two side cameras?

contexts.context: The excerpt reports assembly-policy experiments, not fixed third-person camera layouts. Vision was critical: ablations compared proprioception-only with visual depth, and default models achieved 54.5% (90-object generalist) and 79.8% (100 specialists), versus lower visual-ablated results (39.6% and 46.4%). An alternative camera placement offered a better grasped-plug view but increased occlusion; results support the default because occlusion causes failures, especially with large plugs obscuring sockets. Across 100 assemblies, the method achieved 79.78% success versus AutoMate’s 70.31%, with explicitly noted performance degradation on more occluded objects.

answer.formatted_answer:
Question: Setup: a tabletop 6-DOF robot arm (AgileX PiPER, about 0.63 m reach, fingertips reach about 0.76 m at table height) on a 1.29 x 1.36 m table against a wall. We want fixed RGB cameras (Raspberry Pi Camera Module 3 Wide, 102 x 67 deg field of view, 4608 x 2592 px) that (a) triangulate the gripper fingertips to check the arm's joint-angle kinematics (detect drift of a few mm), (b) show whether the workspace is clear, and (c) may later feed learned visuomotor policies. Current proposal: one camera about 1.2 m above the table looking straight down, one about 0.8 m from the arm base past the table end the arm faces at joint 1 = 0, about 0.42 m up and tilted 19 deg down, and a third low camera on the room-side table edge looking toward the wall. Which fixed third-person camera viewpoints do tabletop robot-manipulation datasets and benchmarks use (for example ALOHA / ALOHA 2, Mobile ALOHA, DROID, BridgeData V2, robomimic, FurnitureBench, RH20T, Open X-Embodiment, LeRobot SO-100/SO-101, AgileX Cobot Magic), including camera heights, distances and angles where reported, and what quantitative evidence exists on how viewpoint choice (overhead/top-down, front, side, over-the-shoulder) and the number of fixed views affect visuomotor policy success and robustness to camera shifts? Does the evidence support or contradict an overhead camera plus two side cameras?

# Fixed-camera viewpoints for a tabletop PiPER

**Bottom line.** An overhead camera plus two oblique cameras is a defensible design for *workspace monitoring and independent fingertip triangulation*. It is **not** an arrangement that the policy-learning literature has established as uniquely optimal. Published systems commonly combine a global external view with a front or low-angle view; many also use wrist views. Their papers generally do **not** report reproducible camera heights, distances, or pitch angles. Place the third camera to supply *different visibility and triangulation geometry*, rather than simply another similar-looking image. (zhao2023learningfinegrainedbimanual pages 2-3, chuang2025activevisionmight pages 3-4, khazatsky2024droidalargescale pages 3-4, chuang2025activevisionmight pages 5-6)

## What the cited platforms actually use

| Platform | Reported external viewpoints; distinction from wrist cameras | Published mounting dimensions? |
|---|---|---|
| **Original ALOHA** | One **top** and one **front** fixed Logitech C922x webcam; two additional webcams on the follower wrists. The paper describes four 640 × 480 RGB inputs, not three fixed scene cameras. | No numeric camera height, standoff, or tilt in the cited paper. Its figure’s **60 cm and 50 cm markings depict workspace dimensions**, not camera-mount specifications. (zhao2023learningfinegrainedbimanual pages 3-4, zhao2023learningfinegrainedbimanual pages 2-3) |
| **ALOHA 2** | In the documented ALOHA-2-based AV-ALOHA setup, two fixed Intel RealSense D405 cameras are mounted at the **top and bottom** of the frame, yielding high- and low-angle views; two other D405s are wrist-mounted. AV-ALOHA adds a separately movable stereo camera, which is *not* a fixed viewpoint. | No numeric mount geometry in that account. (chuang2025activevisionmight pages 3-4) |
| **Mobile ALOHA** | One robot-**top-mounted** scene camera and two wrist cameras. The top camera moves *with the mobile base*, so it is not a stationary room camera. | No camera mounting coordinates reported. The figure’s **65–200 cm** numbers are arm reach heights, **100 cm** is arm extension, and **140 cm** is system height—not camera height. (fu2401mobilealohalearning pages 2-4) |
| **DROID** | Two adjustable, exterior, table-mounted **ZED 2 stereo camera units**, plus one wrist-mounted ZED Mini stereo unit. Collectors select external views for each scene, calibrate them, and sometimes move and recalibrate them during data collection. Two stereo units yield four exterior image streams; they are not four independent camera *locations*. | No universal height, distance, or tilt: placement deliberately varies. Extrinsic matrices are recorded for the exterior cameras. (khazatsky2024droidalargescale pages 3-4, khazatsky2024droidalargescale pages 13-15) |
| **RH20T** | **8–10 global cameras** and **1–2 in-hand cameras** per collection platform, with calibrated, synchronized multiview RGB-D observations. This is unusually sensor-rich, not a recommendation to fit ten cameras to a small table. | Camera poses are calibrated per setup; no single standard height/angle is specified in the passages examined. (fang2024rh20tacomprehensive pages 4-5) |
| **Open X-Embodiment** | An **aggregation of different institutions and robot embodiments**, not a physical rig with a standard front, overhead, or shoulder placement. | No collection-wide camera height or tilt can be assigned. (collaboration2310openxembodimentrobotic pages 2-3) |
| **LeRobot SO-100/SO-101** | Robot platforms supported by a **camera-configurable software and dataset ecosystem**, not a standardized camera-mounted benchmark. Community datasets can therefore have different views and camera counts. | No universal SO-10X camera pose follows from the LeRobot paper. (cadene2026lerobotanopensource pages 5-7) |
| **AgileX Cobot Magic** | Published experiments identify an **ALOHA-style bimanual platform**; its use does not itself specify the scene cameras for every experiment. | No defensible platform-wide mounting coordinates in the evidence examined. (wu2024robomindbenchmarkon pages 3-4) |
| **BridgeData V2; robomimic; FurnitureBench** | These names do **not** establish a transferable physical camera pose: robomimic is a simulated demonstration benchmark, whereas the other two involve particular real collection/evaluation setups. The indexed primary papers for these three were not available in this search; I cannot verify a precise fixed-view count or mounting layout for them from the retrieved primary text. | **Do not treat an uncited height or angle attributed to any of these as a published specification.** |

The especially relevant precedent for your layout is **ALOHA 2’s fixed high-plus-low views**, whereas DROID favors **two independently placeable exterior units** and careful per-scene calibration. Neither is a controlled test of your proposed overhead-plus-two-sides configuration. (chuang2025activevisionmight pages 3-4, khazatsky2024droidalargescale pages 3-4)

## Quantitative evidence: view *information* matters more than a universal view ranking

**Camera count and occlusion.** AV-ALOHA trained ACT policies with seven combinations of fixed scene (“Static”), wrist, and *actively repositioned* (“AV”) observations. For the relatively visible simulated **slot-insertion** task, full-task success was **66% Static**, **78% Static + Wrist**, but **36% AV + Static + Wrist**. For **hooking a package**, it was **44% Static**, **30% Static + Wrist**, and **24% with all three sources**. Conversely, for visually challenging **threading**, it was **30% Static**, **52% AV**, and **52% AV + Wrist**; for the real **hidden-pick** task, **40% Static** versus **60% AV + Wrist**, but **15% with all three**. Thus, *more camera inputs are not automatically better*, and views that reveal an otherwise hidden target can be disproportionately useful. These comparisons involve moving cameras and an active-camera control problem—not an ablation of two versus three **fixed** exterior cameras. Simulation results selected the best among 12 checkpoints and used 50 rollouts per checkpoint; real-task configurations used 20 rollouts. (chuang2025activevisionmight pages 5-6, chuang2025activevisionmight pages 4-5, chuang2025activevisionmight pages 3-4)

In a separate multi-view world-model study, adding a **left-shoulder view** to **front + wrist** did **not substantially improve** performance on three evaluated tasks. That is useful evidence of diminishing returns, but it does not test whether adding a *fixed low side view to a top-down-only PiPER rig* helps. (seo2023multiviewmaskedworld pages 19-20)

**Front versus oblique/side.** A 2026 StereoPolicy simulation study evaluated **ten external camera angles** on ToolHang. Relative to a monocular policy, stereo fusion’s reported gains were **18 percentage points at frontview** and **14 points at elevated frontview**; side views benefited less, with the authors attributing this to poorer overlap and self-occlusion. This compares *stereo and monocular methods at each view*, **not** absolute success for overhead versus front versus side; it does not establish that a front camera is always best. On ToolHang with 200 demonstrations, removing wrist observations reduced the stereo policy from **96% to 94%**, while an RGB comparison fell **90% to 86%**. Those figures likewise do not imply that two widely separated Pi camera units will behave like a closely spaced, explicitly fused stereo pair. (han2026stereopolicyimprovingrobotic pages 7-9, han2026stereopolicyimprovingrobotic pages 22-24)

**Shifts after training.** Camera placement is a genuine deployment variable. In a real *cup-on-saucer* test, a policy trained on one third-person pose plus a wrist camera achieved **4/40 full-task successes** aggregated over four changed exterior viewpoints. Novel-view augmentation improved aggregate success to **14/50**, or **20/50** when its view generator was additionally adapted on DROID data. These denominators and viewpoint sets are **not identical**—the unaugmented policy’s fifth-camera result was omitted—so interpret the comparison as evidence of brittleness and useful augmentation, not a clean percentage-point estimate for a specified camera displacement. (tian2024viewinvariantpolicylearning pages 7-8)

In the Colosseum simulated perturbation protocol, front and shoulder cameras’ positions can each change by up to **0.1 m per coordinate** and Euler angles by up to **0.05 rad per coordinate** (about **2.9°**); its real extension also changes and recalibrates the front-camera position. These are *test perturbation ranges*, **not recommended mounting tolerances**. In a separate fixed-camera training study, a conventional simulated behavior-cloning policy scored **0%** on easy and hard camera shifts in three evaluated tasks despite canonical successes of **51.7–63.3%**; a different object-centric 3D method retained task-dependent nonzero success. Because the methods and representations differ, this tests robustness, not an overhead-versus-side ranking. (pumacay2024thecolosseuma pages 4-5, pumacay2024thecolosseuma pages 5-7, zhu2310learninggeneralizablemanipulation pages 6-7)

Evidence specifically for **over-the-shoulder** views is also conditional. A 2026 study deliberately sampled two over-the-shoulder cameras and a wrist view, randomizing calibrated RGB-D camera poses during training. On its Cabinet simulation, its geometry-grounded policy attained **64.4 normalized opening** with randomized cameras versus **39.5** for a camera-conditioned comparison; **normalized opening is not a task-success percentage**. It requires calibrated extrinsics and depth and therefore does not directly predict performance from three uncalibrated RGB-only cameras. (nakura2026anempiricalstudy pages 4-5, nakura2026anempiricalstudy pages 5-6)

## Implications for the proposed geometry

**Overhead at 1.2 m.** Using the stated **102° × 67°** field of view and an ideal rectilinear, level camera, table-plane coverage centered on its optical axis is approximately **2 × 1.2 tan(51°) = 2.96 m** horizontally and **2 × 1.2 tan(33.5°) = 1.59 m** vertically. This nominally exceeds the **1.29 × 1.36 m** tabletop when the **67° axis follows the 1.36 m dimension**, with only about **0.12 m margin at each end** of that dimension if centered. To fit the full 1.36 m in the narrow axis, the ideal minimum height is about **1.03 m**; the 1.2 m proposal therefore has limited tolerance for decentering, tall objects, an elevated gripper, or a narrower effective field after distortion correction. These are *geometric calculations from the specifications in your question*, not published policy results. An overhead image gives excellent table-plane context but cannot, on its own, resolve fingertip height from a single image.

**End-facing camera at 0.42 m height, 0.8 m from the base.** Its nominal optical-axis drop over **0.8 m** at **19°** is only **0.28 m**. If it is aimed toward a table-plane point near the base, the required declination is approximately **arctan(0.42/0.8) = 27.7°**, not 19°. More importantly, at **19°** the *bottom* vertical field boundary points **52.5° downward**. At the base’s range, that boundary intersects the tabletop only **0.33 m horizontally from the camera**; whether the important near edge or floor is visible depends on where the camera actually sits relative to the tabletop. Conversely, the top boundary points **14.5° upward**, providing room to see elevated gripper positions. These angles do **not** by themselves determine usable coverage: roll orientation, which sensor dimension is horizontal, image distortion, clipping by the table edge, and the base’s offset from that edge must be checked with sample frames. Aim at the **center of the fingertip’s *3D operating volume***, not simply at the arm base. Calculations here use your stated pose and FOV, not a reported mounting geometry from a dataset.

**Third, low room-side edge camera.** Keep it sufficiently **oblique and separated in azimuth** from the end-facing view that a fingertip obscured by the gripper, arm, or an object in one side image remains visible in another. A low view contributes evidence of clearance, contact height, and the near side of objects that top-down imagery may conceal; an *extremely* low grazing angle instead risks table-edge occlusion and overlapping fingertips. Position and angle should be chosen by measuring visibility of **both fingertips** across sampled joint configurations, rather than by copying a platform label such as “sideview.” High/low viewpoint complementarity is supported by ALOHA 2’s hardware choice; the need to inspect occlusion is supported by the controlled view experiments. (chuang2025activevisionmight pages 3-4, chuang2025activevisionmight pages 5-6, han2026stereopolicyimprovingrobotic pages 7-9)

**For the few-millimetre drift objective, camera count alone is insufficient.** A back-of-envelope ideal overhead image scale is roughly **2.96 m/4608 ≈ 0.64 mm per pixel** along the wide axis and **1.59 m/2592 ≈ 0.61 mm per pixel** along the narrow axis *at table height*. Those are projected sampling pitches, **not 3D accuracy**: fingertip localization, lens distortion, limited stereo intersection angles, exposure/motion blur, synchronization, and robot-to-camera calibration introduce further error. Calibrate intrinsics and distortion for the actual focus setting, estimate each fixed camera’s extrinsics in one **table/robot-base frame**, and verify *held-out 3D fingertip errors* throughout the reachable volume against a separately measured target. DROID’s repeated extrinsic calibration and RH20T’s multiview camera-to-robot calibration illustrate the distinction between recording extra images and obtaining comparable 3D measurements. Do not fit camera extrinsics to the same potentially drifting joint-angle kinematics you intend to audit without an independent check: doing so can absorb the drift into the calibration. (khazatsky2024droidalargescale pages 3-4, fang2024rh20tacomprehensive pages 4-5)

**Recommendation.** Install the overhead camera for global clearance and two *nonredundant* oblique cameras for fingertip visibility and depth geometry; the proposed end-facing plus room-side arrangement is a reasonable **starting configuration**, not a literature-validated optimum. First map each camera’s actual field of view and fingertip occlusion over the robot’s working poses; next calibrate and quantify 3D reconstruction error before claiming detection of a few millimetres of kinematic drift. For learned policies, retain consistent camera poses between demonstrations and deployment, and compare overhead-only, overhead + best side, and all three **on your own tasks**. Existing ablations demonstrate that task-dependent visibility helps, added views sometimes add nothing or hurt, and untrained camera shifts can be severe; they do not support a universal prescription of exactly three fixed views. (chuang2025activevisionmight pages 5-6, seo2023multiviewmaskedworld pages 19-20, tian2024viewinvariantpolicylearning pages 7-8, zhu2310learninggeneralizablemanipulation pages 6-7)

info.query: Setup: a tabletop 6-DOF robot arm (AgileX PiPER, about 0.63 m reach, fingertips reach about 0.76 m at table height) on a 1.29 x 1.36 m table against a wall. We want fixed RGB cameras (Raspberry Pi Camera Module 3 Wide, 102 x 67 deg field of view, 4608 x 2592 px) that (a) triangulate the gripper fingertips to check the arm's joint-angle kinematics (detect drift of a few mm), (b) show whether the workspace is clear, and (c) may later feed learned visuomotor policies. Current proposal: one camera about 1.2 m above the table looking straight down, one about 0.8 m from the arm base past the table end the arm faces at joint 1 = 0, about 0.42 m up and tilted 19 deg down, and a third low camera on the room-side table edge looking toward the wall. Which fixed third-person camera viewpoints do tabletop robot-manipulation datasets and benchmarks use (for example ALOHA / ALOHA 2, Mobile ALOHA, DROID, BridgeData V2, robomimic, FurnitureBench, RH20T, Open X-Embodiment, LeRobot SO-100/SO-101, AgileX Cobot Magic), including camera heights, distances and angles where reported, and what quantitative evidence exists on how viewpoint choice (overhead/top-down, front, side, over-the-shoulder) and the number of fixed views affect visuomotor policy success and robustness to camera shifts? Does the evidence support or contradict an overhead camera plus two side cameras?
